title: Aspen Park CO well depth and drilling cost
meta_description: In Aspen Park, median well depth is 305 ft and median yield is 5 gpm. See what that means for drilling costs and well reliability in this mountain area.
h1: Water wells in Aspen Park, Colorado
intro_html:
Aspen Park sits in fractured mountain bedrock, so wells here are deeper and more variable than in the plains. The state has records for thousands of nearby wells, with enough data to give you a realistic idea of how deep you’re likely to drill, how much water to expect, and what that means for your budget.

Below is what the local well history shows for Aspen Park and nearby spots like Conifer, Evergreen, and Indian Hills, plus some practical advice if you’re buying or planning to build on a well-dependent lot.

sections.heading: How deep wells run around Aspen Park
sections.html:
Within about 5 miles of Aspen Park, the median well depth is 305 feet. The middle half of wells fall between 195 and 483 feet, so most drillers will bid with a wide allowance on depth. About 35% of wells are 100–300 feet, 41% run 300–600 feet, and 15% go past 600 feet, up to a local maximum of 1,703 feet.

All of this is in fractured bedrock (mostly unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifers, plus some Fractured Crystalline and Fractured Granite). That kind of geology is hit-or-miss: one parcel may hit good water at 250 feet while the neighbor needs 500+ feet. When you price a lot in Aspen Park or Conifer, you really want to look up nearby well depths, not just averages.

sections.heading: Well yield: how much water is typical here
sections.html:
For wells with reported pump tests, the median yield is 5.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 3.0 and 8.3 gpm. About 38% of wells test between 1 and 5 gpm, 52% land between 5 and 15 gpm, and only 6% report more than 15 gpm. Low producers under 1 gpm show up in about 4% of records.

For a standard exempt household-use well, anything above about 2–3 gpm is usually workable if the well is constructed properly and you manage storage. Around Aspen Park and Evergreen, most domestic wells are in that 3–8 gpm band. The small share under 1 gpm means truly marginal wells exist, but they’re not the norm; still, check the specific permit history for your parcel.

sections.heading: Water levels and long-term trend in Aspen Park
sections.html:
Where static water level is reported, the median depth to water is about 80 feet, with the middle half between 35 and 150 feet below ground surface. So even when total depth runs 200–400 feet, the water column often starts much shallower than the bottom of the hole.

By decade, median water levels have shifted. In the 1960s they were around 40 feet, then 60 in the 1970s and 50 in the 1980s. The 1990s jump to about 135 feet, followed by 120 in the 2000s and 100 in both the 2010s and 2020s. That pattern suggests water levels are generally deeper now than in the 1960s–1980s, but not in a steady free-fall. It’s another reason to review the specific well logs closest to your property in Aspen Park or Morrison.

sections.heading: Who drilled all these wells, and when
sections.html:
This area has a long well history, with 11,280 permits in the state records and 7,605 of those marked as constructed. The big push came in the 1970s with 3,186 permits, then 1,774 in the 1980s and 2,254 in the 1990s. Activity tapered to 1,028 in the 2000s, 439 in the 2010s, and 286 so far in the 2020s, with permits still being issued through 2025.

Most permits are for domestic or household use (about 93%), with small shares for stock, monitoring, and effectively no irrigation. The main drillers on record around Aspen Park are Living Water Systems Inc. (Goble, Robert), Aspen Drilling Company Inc (Beery, Leroy J.), and Walton. If you’re buying an older home in Brook Forest or Pine, pull the original permit and driller’s log; it often tells you depth, yield, and construction details.

sections.heading: What a new well is likely to cost in Aspen Park
sections.html:
Drilling here is through fractured mountain bedrock like granite and gneiss. Typical drilling rates run about $65–$100 per foot. At the local median depth of 305 feet, that puts the drilled hole itself around $19,800–$30,500. By the time you add pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical, a finished domestic well commonly runs in the $25,800–$42,500 range.

Because the middle half of wells stretches from 195 to 483 feet, smart budgeting plans for the upper end of that range, especially on higher or rougher sites. Lots in areas like Indian Hills and Evergreen with similar fractured rock can show the same variability, so I recommend running numbers on a 400–500 foot worst-case unless nearby logs show consistently shallower wells.

sections.heading: Local risks: low yield, contamination, and siting
sections.html:
In this part of Jefferson County, the main technical risk is variable yield from fractured rock. With 4% of wells under 1 gpm and 15% deeper than 600 feet, there’s a non-trivial chance of a deep, low-producing well on a given parcel. Proper well siting and realistic drilling allowances in the contract matter.

On the water quality side, there are mapped environmental concerns in the broader 10-mile area: about 29 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 45 historic mine features, and 51 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. That doesn’t mean your specific well is contaminated, but it does mean testing should be routine: basic potability, metals, and PFAS where appropriate. When planning septic, keep good separation from your well and pay attention to slopes and setbacks if you’re building on tight mountain lots.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a well lot in Aspen Park
sections.html:
If you’re buying a home on an existing well, pull the Colorado DWR permit and well construction report. Around Aspen Park and Conifer, you want to confirm actual depth, reported yield, and static water level against the area norms of 305 feet and about 5 gpm. Ask for recent water-quality tests, especially given the regional PFAS and mine history.

For vacant land, look up at least three nearby wells within a half-mile in similar terrain. Compare their depths (often 195–483 feet) and yields (commonly 3.0–8.3 gpm). Make sure your purchase contract addresses what happens if the new well needs to go much deeper than expected or comes in low-yield. In over-appropriated basins, talk with your water attorney or engineer early about permit type and any augmentation requirements.

faq.q: How deep are water wells in Aspen Park, Colorado?
faq.a: State records within about 5 miles of Aspen Park show a median well depth of 305 feet. The middle half of wells are between 195 and 483 feet. About 35% of wells are 100–300 feet deep, 41% are 300–600 feet, and 15% extend beyond 600 feet, with the deepest recorded at 1,703 feet. Your specific lot could land anywhere in that range depending on the local fractures.

faq.q: How much water do Aspen Park wells typically produce?
faq.a: For wells that report pump tests near Aspen Park, the median yield is 5.0 gallons per minute. The middle half fall between 3.0 and 8.3 gpm. About 38% of wells test between 1 and 5 gpm, 52% are between 5 and 15 gpm, and only 4% are under 1 gpm. That yield range is usually adequate for domestic use if the well and plumbing system are designed correctly.

faq.q: Are water levels dropping in wells around Aspen Park?
faq.a: Median static water levels have generally gotten deeper compared to the 1960s–1980s, but not in a simple straight drop. Decade medians were about 40 feet in the 1960s, 60 in the 1970s, 50 in the 1980s, then 135 in the 1990s. They eased to around 120 feet in the 2000s and 100 feet in the 2010s and 2020s. So water is deeper than early records, but recent decades show some stabilization.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Aspen Park?
faq.a: In fractured mountain bedrock around Aspen Park, typical drilling rates run about $65–$100 per foot. At the local median depth of 305 feet, the drilled hole alone works out to roughly $19,800–$30,500. Once you add pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work, a complete domestic well commonly totals about $25,800–$42,500. Budget higher if nearby wells are consistently deeper than 305 feet.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Aspen Park, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety depends on the individual well. The area has about 29 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 45 historic mine features, and 51 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within roughly 10 miles, so water quality is something to check, not assume. Before relying on any well near Aspen Park, have it tested for basic potability, metals, and PFAS where advised, and review the well’s construction and maintenance history.
